question: What amount is appropriated for the FDA Salaries and Expenses account in FY2026, and what are the major allowed uses?

division_answers.division: AGRICULTURE, RURAL DEVELOPMENT, FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION, AND RELATED AGENCIES
division_answers.answer:
### [AG] AGRICULTURE, RURAL DEVELOPMENT, FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION, AND RELATED AGENCIES
$6,957,972,000 [[num:src_ag_cee4dfd9_de7e_40f0_b82e_f896328a8490_1]] is appropriated for FDA Salaries and Expenses in FY2026.

Major allowed uses include:
- Human Foods Program and related field activities, including inspections, investigations, and import operations [[num:src_ag_b9334bc1_3b42_4f87_9b47_7824d5cc66d0_2]].
- Center for Drug Evaluation and Research and related field activities [[num:src_ag_b9334bc1_3b42_4f87_9b47_7824d5cc66d0_4]].
- Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research [[num:src_ag_b9334bc1_3b42_4f87_9b47_7824d5cc66d0_6]], Center for Veterinary Medicine [[num:src_ag_b9334bc1_3b42_4f87_9b47_7824d5cc66d0_7]], Center for Devices and Radiological Health [[num:src_ag_b9334bc1_3b42_4f87_9b47_7824d5cc66d0_8]], National Center for Toxicological Research [[num:src_ag_b9334bc1_3b42_4f87_9b47_7824d5cc66d0_9]], and Center for Tobacco Products [[num:src_ag_b9334bc1_3b42_4f87_9b47_7824d5cc66d0_10]] and related field activities.
- Rent and related activities, including GSA rent and White Oak consolidation [[num:src_ag_c5f1a478_c79a_41c8_b555_a51f9d9639c7_4]] [[num:src_ag_c5f1a478_c79a_41c8_b555_a51f9d9639c7_5]] [[num:src_ag_c5f1a478_c79a_41c8_b555_a51f9d9639c7_6]].
- Other activities, including the Office of the Commissioner, Office of the Chief Scientist, Office of the Chief Medical Officer, and central services [[num:src_ag_c5f1a478_c79a_41c8_b555_a51f9d9639c7_7]].
- Applicable FDA user fees are credited to the account and remain available until expended.

division_answers.answer:
### [AG] AGRICULTURE, RURAL DEVELOPMENT, FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION, AND RELATED AGENCIES
The USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service is appropriated $1,215,200,000 [[num:src_ag_edc59832_2cb3_4b5e_8135_dc08af3b46e9_1]] for necessary expenses to carry out services authorized by the Federal Meat Inspection Act, the Poultry Products Inspection Act, and the Egg Products Inspection Act, including not to exceed $10,000 [[num:src_ag_edc59832_2cb3_4b5e_8135_dc08af3b46e9_2]] for representation allowances [[num:src_ag_edc59832_2cb3_4b5e_8135_dc08af3b46e9_1]].

It funds:
- laboratory accreditation [[num:src_ag_edc59832_2cb3_4b5e_8135_dc08af3b46e9_3]]
- the Public Health Data Communication Infrastructure system
- inspections and enforcement related to the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act
- implementation of section 11016 of Public Law 110-246

In addition, $1,000,000 [[num:src_ag_edc59832_2cb3_4b5e_8135_dc08af3b46e9_3]] may be credited to the account from laboratory accreditation fees.

It funds:
- laboratory accreditation [[num:src_ag_edc59832_2cb3_4b5e_8135_dc08af3b46e9_3]]
- the Public Health Data Communication Infrastructure system
- inspections and enforcement related to the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act
- implementation of section 11016 of Public Law 110-246

In addition, $1,000,000 [[num:src_ag_edc59832_2cb3_4b5e_8135_dc08af3b46e9_3]] may be credited to the account from laboratory accreditation fees.

### [CJS] COMMERCE, JUSTICE, SCIENCE, AND RELATED AGENCIES

NASA Science is appropriated $7,250,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_eb913c86_3ab8_478b_b5b6_749cc2964621_1]] in FY2026, to remain available until September 30, 2027.

Funding is available for necessary expenses in the conduct and support of science research and development activities, including research, development, operations, support, and services; maintenance and repair; facility planning and design; space flight, spacecraft control, and communications activities; program management; personnel and related costs; travel expenses; and purchase, hire, charter, maintenance, and operation of passenger motor vehicles and mission and administrative aircraft.

division_answers.answer:
### [AG] AGRICULTURE, RURAL DEVELOPMENT, FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION, AND RELATED AGENCIES
Bottom line: USDA’s Rural Utilities Service controls the Rural Water and Waste Disposal Program Account; a clean all-in total is not available because the extracted facts mix direct loan authority, guaranteed loans, grant/cost funding, community project funding, and technical assistance.

Key buckets:
- Rural Utilities Service — Rural Water and Waste Disposal Program Account: $1,015,000,000 [[num:src_ag_160a4a3e_e145_4648_b90b_06162c1802d7_1]] for direct loans and $50,000,000 [[num:src_ag_160a4a3e_e145_4648_b90b_06162c1802d7_2]] for guaranteed loans for rural water, waste water, waste disposal, and solid waste management; the account also provides $445,864,564 [[num:src_ag_160a4a3e_e145_4648_b90b_06162c1802d7_3]] for the cost of direct loans, loan guarantees and grants, plus $110,488,564 [[num:src_ag_24476027_1e00_4a79_bfd0_f22f7a3ed794_1]] for community project funding/Congressionally Directed Spending.
- Same heading, technical assistance: $35,000,000 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_1]] for technical assistance grants for rural water and waste systems, including $10,000,000 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_2]] for a qualified nonprofit multi-State regional technical assistance organization and at least $800,000 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_3]] for tribal water-system technical assistance; plus $23,900,000 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_4]] for a circuit rider program.

Local caveat: I did not add any adjacent rural-development accounts that are not explicitly water/wastewater, and I did not sum the nested sub-buckets to avoid double counting.

division_answers.division: DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, ENVIRONMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES
division_answers.answer:
### [INT] DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, ENVIRONMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES

Bottom line: EPA controls the main rural water/wastewater money here through the State and Tribal Assistance Grants account and the Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Program, but no single clean additive total is available because the division mixes grant appropriations, loan subsidy cost, and loan principal authority.

Key buckets:
- **EPA — State and Tribal Assistance Grants:** $4,409,609,000 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_1]] for environmental programs and infrastructure assistance. Within it: $1,638,861,000 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_2]] for Clean Water SRF capitalization grants; $1,126,101,000 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_3]] for Drinking Water SRF capitalization grants; $892,762,272 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_4]] for Clean Water SRF project construction; and $715,364,627 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_5]] for Drinking Water SRF project construction. The SRF rules also require 10% of Clean Water SRF funds and 14% of Drinking Water SRF funds to go to additional subsidy.
- **EPA — Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Program:** $64,634,000 [[num:src_int_23bdcd4f_a5f3_4aea_a8f2_37873ef6c487_1]] for the cost of direct and guaranteed loans; the funds support up to $12,500,000,000 [[num:src_int_23bdcd4f_a5f3_4aea_a8f2_37873ef6c487_2]] in total loan principal, with a $5,000,000 [[num:src_int_23bdcd4f_a5f3_4aea_a8f2_37873ef6c487_3]] set-aside for state infrastructure financing authorities.
- **EPA — targeted water/wastewater grants and special projects:** $39,000,000 [[num:src_int_68c231bc_233c_49a7_9433_ff67261f494c_1]] for Alaska rural and Alaska Native Villages; $35,000,000 for high-priority water and wastewater facilities along the U.S.-Mexico border; $2,250,000 [[num:src_int_43a8dd3d_d24d_47a3_afa5_b1919462588e_1]] under Safe Drinking Water Act section 1459F; $4,000,000 [[num:src_int_43a8dd3d_d24d_47a3_afa5_b1919462588e_2]] under America’s Water Infrastructure Act section 2001; $2,000,000 [[num:src_int_43a8dd3d_d24d_47a3_afa5_b1919462588e_3]] under IIJA section 50217(b); and $3,500,000 [[num:src_int_43a8dd3d_d24d_47a3_afa5_b1919462588e_4]] under Clean Water Act section 124.

Local caveat: I did not add the SRF additional-subsidy percentages or other internal set-asides into the account totals to avoid double counting.

division_answers.division: ENERGY AND WATER DEVELOPMENT AND RELATED AGENCIES
division_answers.answer:
### [EWD] ENERGY AND WATER DEVELOPMENT AND RELATED AGENCIES
Bottom line: No clean FY2026 rural water/wastewater total is available from the direct facts because the controllable items are a WIFIA loan-principal cap and a separate rural project authorization, not a single additive account total.

Key buckets:
- Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Program Account: direct loan and loan guarantee authority with total loan principal not to exceed $500,000,000 [[num:src_ewd_de16a15b_0ec3_40a9_b8e4_af9d7be19e3b_1]] for projects including rural water or wastewater infrastructure.
- Northwestern New Mexico Rural Water Projects Act, section 209(a)(1): authorization is amended from $870,000,000 [[num:src_ewd_2c53e5b7_445f_4a58_9f31_e75503c34d77_1]] to $1,815,000,000 [[num:src_ewd_2c53e5b7_445f_4a58_9f31_e75503c34d77_2]]; this is a direct rural water project amount.

Local caveat: The WIFIA item is loan authority for qualifying projects, while the Northwestern New Mexico item is a specific project authorization, so they should not be added as one total.

final_answer:
## Answer
No single clean FY2026 total is available because the identified funding mixes appropriated grant/subsidy amounts, loan authority, loan-subsidy cost, principal caps, and a project authorization. The main controlling accounts are USDA Rural Utilities Service’s Rural Water and Waste Disposal Program Account, EPA’s State and Tribal Assistance Grants and Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Program Account, and a separate Energy and Water Development WIFIA-related authority plus the Northwestern New Mexico Rural Water Projects Act authorization.

## Topic-Specific or Targeted Funding
### USDA Rural Utilities Service — Rural Water and Waste Disposal Program Account [AG]
- Appropriated cost/grant/subsidy: $445,864,564 [[num:src_ag_160a4a3e_e145_4648_b90b_06162c1802d7_3]] for the cost of direct loans, loan guarantees, and grants for rural water, wastewater, waste disposal, and solid waste management.
- Loan authority:
  - Direct loans: $1,015,000,000 [[num:src_ag_160a4a3e_e145_4648_b90b_06162c1802d7_1]]
  - Guaranteed loans: $50,000,000 [[num:src_ag_160a4a3e_e145_4648_b90b_06162c1802d7_2]]
- Grant reservation:
  - Community project funding/Congressionally Directed Spending: $110,488,564 [[num:src_ag_24476027_1e00_4a79_bfd0_f22f7a3ed794_1]]
- Key identified suballocations within/under this account:
  - Direct loans within the appropriated amount: $51,476,000 [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_2]]
  - Water and waste direct one percent loans for distressed communities: $3,876,000 [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_3]]
  - Section 306E rural utilities program: $5,000,000 [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_4]]
  - Subgrants for individually owned household decentralized wastewater systems: $1,000,000 [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_5]]
  - Loans and grants including water and waste disposal systems: $60,000,000 [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_6]]

### USDA Rural Utilities Service — Technical assistance for rural water and waste systems [AG]
- Grant reservation: $35,000,000 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_1]] for technical assistance grants for rural water and waste systems.
- Key identified suballocations within/under this account:
  - Qualified nonprofit multi-State regional technical assistance organization: $10,000,000 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_2]]
  - Tribal rural water-system technical assistance: $800,000 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_3]]
  - Circuit rider program for rural water systems: $23,900,000 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_4]]

### EPA — State and Tribal Assistance Grants [INT]
- Appropriated cost/grant/subsidy: $1,638,861,000 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_2]] for Clean Water State Revolving Fund capitalization grants.
- Appropriated cost/grant/subsidy: $1,126,101,000 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_3]] for Drinking Water State Revolving Fund capitalization grants.
- Key identified suballocations within/under this account:
  - Clean Water SRF set-aside for specified projects: $892,762,272 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_4]]
  - Drinking Water SRF set-aside for specified projects: $715,364,627 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_5]]

### EPA — Targeted water and wastewater grants [INT]
- Appropriated cost/grant/subsidy: $39,000,000 [[num:src_int_68c231bc_233c_49a7_9433_ff67261f494c_1]] for Alaska rural water/wastewater.
- Appropriated cost/grant/subsidy: $35,000,000 [[num:src_int_d34f361a_4aeb_40bb_8589_d2bba8dbf995_1]] for water and wastewater facilities along the U.S.-Mexico border.
- Appropriated cost/grant/subsidy:
  - Safe Drinking Water Act grants: $2,250,000 [[num:src_int_43a8dd3d_d24d_47a3_afa5_b1919462588e_1]]
  - America’s Water Infrastructure Act grants: $4,000,000 [[num:src_int_43a8dd3d_d24d_47a3_afa5_b1919462588e_2]]
  - IIJA water infrastructure grants: $2,000,000 [[num:src_int_43a8dd3d_d24d_47a3_afa5_b1919462588e_3]]
  - Clean Water Act section 124 grants: $3,500,000 [[num:src_int_43a8dd3d_d24d_47a3_afa5_b1919462588e_4]]

## Broader Related Funding
### EPA — Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Program Account [INT]
- Appropriated cost/grant/subsidy: $64,634,000 [[num:src_int_23bdcd4f_a5f3_4aea_a8f2_37873ef6c487_1]] for the cost of direct and guaranteed loans.
- Cap/limitation: $12,500,000,000 [[num:src_int_23bdcd4f_a5f3_4aea_a8f2_37873ef6c487_2]] in total loan principal.
- Key identified suballocations within/under this account:
  - Set-aside for state infrastructure financing authorities: $5,000,000 [[num:src_int_23bdcd4f_a5f3_4aea_a8f2_37873ef6c487_3]]

### Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Program Account [EWD]
- Cap/limitation: $500,000,000 [[num:src_ewd_de16a15b_0ec3_40a9_b8e4_af9d7be19e3b_1]] in total loan principal for projects including rural water or wastewater infrastructure.

## Identified But Not Cleanly Topic-Specific
### EPA — State and Tribal Assistance Grants [INT]
- $4,409,609,000 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_1]] is the total account amount, but only part of that broader account is specifically identified here for water infrastructure.

### Northwestern New Mexico Rural Water Projects Act [EWD]
- The authorization is amended from $870,000,000 [[num:src_ewd_2c53e5b7_445f_4a58_9f31_e75503c34d77_1]] to $1,815,000,000 [[num:src_ewd_2c53e5b7_445f_4a58_9f31_e75503c34d77_2]], but this is a project authorization rather than a clean FY2026 appropriated funding amount.

## Caveats
- Do not add account totals to their nested set-asides, community project funding, or technical-assistance suballocations; several listed amounts sit within broader headings.
- Do not add loan authority, loan principal caps, or loan-subsidy cost to grant/subsidy appropriations as if they were the same type of funding.
- EPA’s SRF capitalization grants are broad national water-infrastructure funding streams that can support rural systems, but they are not rural-only accounts.
- The Energy and Water Development WIFIA cap and the Northwestern New Mexico project authorization are not directly comparable to USDA or EPA appropriations.

division_answers.answer:
### [THUD] TRANSPORTATION, HOUSING AND URBAN DEVELOPMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES
Bottom line: No clean division total is available from the extracted facts because the FY2026 support for affordable housing, rental assistance, and homelessness services is split across multiple HUD accounts and suballocations rather than one additive funding line.

Key buckets:
- Tenant-based rental assistance: $34,438,557,000 [[num:src_thud_4a3a0d30_b7b3_442e_8ee2_d6e04108d60d_1]] is appropriated, with an additional $4,000,000,000 [[num:src_thud_4a3a0d30_b7b3_442e_8ee2_d6e04108d60d_2]] available Oct. 1, 2025 and $4,000,000,000 [[num:src_thud_4a3a0d30_b7b3_442e_8ee2_d6e04108d60d_3]] available Oct. 1, 2026; of the sums appropriated, $34,957,000,000 [[num:src_thud_4a3a0d30_b7b3_442e_8ee2_d6e04108d60d_4]] is for renewals of expiring Section 8 tenant-based annual contributions contracts. The account also includes $2,835,935,000 [[num:src_thud_5fad2772_9db5_42a0_aaa6_4e599541119b_1]] for administrative and other expenses, with up to $30,000,000 [[num:src_thud_5fad2772_9db5_42a0_aaa6_4e599541119b_2]] for PHAs needing extra admin funds, and a minimum allocation of $2,805,935,000 [[num:src_thud_5fad2772_9db5_42a0_aaa6_4e599541119b_3]] for the CY2026 funding cycle.
- Project-based rental assistance: $18,143,000,000 [[num:src_thud_f1b2363f_5009_4e7f_a53a_19d7a641efa5_1]] is appropriated, with $400,000,000 [[num:src_thud_f1b2363f_5009_4e7f_a53a_19d7a641efa5_2]] previously appropriated available Oct. 1, 2025 and $400,000,000 [[num:src_thud_f1b2363f_5009_4e7f_a53a_19d7a641efa5_3]] available Oct. 1, 2026; unobligated balances from prior housing certificate fund, annual contributions for assisted housing, and project-based rental assistance balances may also be used for renewals or amendments of Section 8 project-based contracts.
- Public housing: the Public Housing Fund receives $8,319,393,000 [[num:src_thud_9841cfd4_18e8_4504_8843_461e06569ba5_1]], including $4,687,393,000 [[num:src_thud_9841cfd4_18e8_4504_8843_461e06569ba5_2]] for the operating fund formula, $337,000,000 [[num:src_thud_9841cfd4_18e8_4504_8843_461e06569ba5_3]] for need-based shortfalls, and $3,200,000,000 [[num:src_thud_9841cfd4_18e8_4504_8843_461e06569ba5_4]] for the capital fund formula.
- Homelessness services: Sec. 244 provides non-competitive renewal of Homeless Assistance Grants projects expiring in the first quarter of calendar year 2026, including youth homelessness demonstration projects, shelter plus care projects, and continuum of care projects; separate direct funding includes $10,000,000 [[num:src_thud_e4156bb6_ba90_4d3d_895c_fabbe74b30cd_1]] for the national homeless data analysis project, $107,000,000 [[num:src_thud_e4156bb6_ba90_4d3d_895c_fabbe74b30cd_2]] for youth homelessness demonstrations, and up to $25,000,000 [[num:src_thud_e4156bb6_ba90_4d3d_895c_fabbe74b30cd_3]] of that amount for youth homelessness system improvement grants.
- Other decision-useful rental-assistance buckets: $287,000,000 [[num:src_thud_853b7fb5_28ff_4aa9_be82_2ff235743a46_1]] is for Section 811 project rental assistance and related supportive services; up to $400,000,000 [[num:src_thud_2941ae6f_a05e_4ee2_ade1_bda259210ed7_1]] is for voucher allocation adjustments and to prevent termination or proration of rental assistance; and $600,622,000 [[num:src_thud_0c6d5767_f51e_4e6c_9007_bde8b65b3780_1]] is for Section 8 rental assistance tied to relocation, replacement, tenant protection, enhanced vouchers, and related displacement-prevention uses.

Local caveat: some of these are account totals, while others are suballocations or renewal authorities inside the same HUD heading, so they should not be summed across bullets.

division_answers.division: TRANSPORTATION, HOUSING AND URBAN DEVELOPMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES
division_answers.answer:
### [THUD] TRANSPORTATION, HOUSING AND URBAN DEVELOPMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES
Bottom line: Airport-related funding is split between Grants-In-Aid for Airports and Airport and Airway Trust Fund liquidation funding; no clean division total is available without double-counting the Grants-In-Aid suballocation.

Key buckets:
- **Grants-In-Aid for Airports** receives $577,356,000 [[num:src_thud_08e7ebfb_009f_4360_b8cf_a3a46fff4355_1]] for airport projects authorized by title 49 and the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024; within that, $542,356,000 [[num:src_thud_fee450f1_68dd_4ce0_8a10_952c9f1247ce_1]] is for Community Project Funding/Congressionally Directed Spending for airports, and up to $35,000,000 [[num:src_thud_fee450f1_68dd_4ce0_8a10_952c9f1247ce_2]] is for discretionary grants for airports, including runway improvements and terminal upgrades.
- **Airport and Airway Trust Fund grants-in-aid** provides $4,000,000,000 [[num:src_thud_31ebccae_5a9f_4e63_8c38_b7c4472f4cfd_1]] for airport planning and development, runway incursion prevention devices and systems, section 41743 grants, and airport safety program administration.

Local caveat: The $542,356,000 [[num:src_thud_fee450f1_68dd_4ce0_8a10_952c9f1247ce_1]] Community Project Funding amount is a suballocation within the $577,356,000 [[num:src_thud_08e7ebfb_009f_4360_b8cf_a3a46fff4355_1]] Grants-In-Aid for Airports account, so it should not be added again.

question: What FY2026 funding is available for local law enforcement, community violence prevention, or police hiring?
expected_divisions: COMMERCE, JUSTICE, SCIENCE, AND RELATED AGENCIES
actual_divisions: COMMERCE, JUSTICE, SCIENCE, AND RELATED AGENCIES
answer_mode_reason: The question asks for FY2026 funding across multiple broad categories (local law enforcement, violence prevention, police hiring), likely spanning multiple accounts/agencies, so a grouped total is needed.

division_answers.division: COMMERCE, JUSTICE, SCIENCE, AND RELATED AGENCIES
division_answers.answer:
### [CJS] COMMERCE, JUSTICE, SCIENCE, AND RELATED AGENCIES
Bottom line: FY2026 CJS includes several direct law-enforcement, police-hiring, and community-violence-prevention funding lines, but no clean division-wide total is available because the figures mix account totals and separate suballocations.

Key buckets:
- Community Oriented Policing Services programs receive $800,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_a2285250_8ebb_40d4_9a2b_ced3cb951f4d_1]]; within that account, $253,093,613 [[num:src_cjs_a2285250_8ebb_40d4_9a2b_ced3cb951f4d_2]] is for hiring and rehiring additional career law enforcement officers, and $32,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_a2285250_8ebb_40d4_9a2b_ced3cb951f4d_3]] is for improving Tribal law enforcement.
- Other direct local-law-enforcement and violence-prevention line items include $84,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_ee257d71_e20a_4bf8_b771_bdb06ef54f09_1]] for initiatives to improve police-community relations, with $15,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_ee257d71_e20a_4bf8_b771_bdb06ef54f09_2]] for body-worn cameras, $19,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_ee257d71_e20a_4bf8_b771_bdb06ef54f09_3]] for justice reinvestment, and $50,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_ee257d71_e20a_4bf8_b771_bdb06ef54f09_4]] for community violence intervention and prevention; plus $53,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_62eafab4_cec8_4428_89f5_1e196c5fa9dc_1]] for STOP School Violence Act grants, $18,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_62eafab4_cec8_4428_89f5_1e196c5fa9dc_2]] for community policing development, $401,406,387 [[num:src_cjs_62eafab4_cec8_4428_89f5_1e196c5fa9dc_3]] for law enforcement technologies and interoperable communications, and $15,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_62eafab4_cec8_4428_89f5_1e196c5fa9dc_4]] for law enforcement de-escalation training.
- Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant program gets $964,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_986f1b11_1c38_4952_8425_6334042e3993_1]], including $12,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_986f1b11_1c38_4952_8425_6334042e3993_2]] for VALOR and $6,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_986f1b11_1c38_4952_8425_6334042e3993_3]] for officer training on responding to mental illness or disabilities; the separate State and Local Law Enforcement Assistance line is $55,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_e8a76109_44b1_471f_9daf_ea3018132572_1]].
- Other targeted grants for local law enforcement include $13,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_3815a4ce_b459_4635_acf9_743d4d84beb0_1]] for Project Safe Neighborhoods, $3,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_3815a4ce_b459_4635_acf9_743d4d84beb0_2]] for a rural violent crime initiative, $30,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_b5ab4f35_dc3c_437a_a1b0_f09cdab66ba5_1]] for the Bulletproof Vest Partnership, $7,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_28b66e70_41bf_4d4d_a751_6fd4fa097898_1]] for the Daniel Anderl Judicial Security and Privacy grant, $5,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_44fc3bd3_fc57_4ba2_b05f_feafe8243a42_1]] for trauma-informed training for law enforcement, $5,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_44fc3bd3_fc57_4ba2_b05f_feafe8243a42_2]] for local law enforcement cybercrime grants, and $50,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_00a7e96c_bb00_46f8_9e9b_d6511c9d284d_1]] for community-based grant programs that may include community violence prevention.

Local caveat: Several of these figures are suballocations within broader programs, so I have not summed them across buckets.

- Other targeted grants for local law enforcement include $13,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_3815a4ce_b459_4635_acf9_743d4d84beb0_1]] for Project Safe Neighborhoods, $3,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_3815a4ce_b459_4635_acf9_743d4d84beb0_2]] for a rural violent crime initiative, $30,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_b5ab4f35_dc3c_437a_a1b0_f09cdab66ba5_1]] for the Bulletproof Vest Partnership, $7,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_28b66e70_41bf_4d4d_a751_6fd4fa097898_1]] for the Daniel Anderl Judicial Security and Privacy grant, $5,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_44fc3bd3_fc57_4ba2_b05f_feafe8243a42_1]] for trauma-informed training for law enforcement, $5,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_44fc3bd3_fc57_4ba2_b05f_feafe8243a42_2]] for local law enforcement cybercrime grants, and $50,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_00a7e96c_bb00_46f8_9e9b_d6511c9d284d_1]] for community-based grant programs that may include community violence prevention.

Local caveat: Several of these figures are suballocations within broader programs, so I have not summed them across buckets.

mapped_chunks.chunk_summary: This chunk shows $2.4 billion is available, including $964 million for the Byrne JAG program, which funds local police hiring and violence prevention.

relevance_facts.fact: For the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant program, $964,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_986f1b11_1c38_4952_8425_6334042e3993_1]] is provided, of which $12,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_986f1b11_1c38_4952_8425_6334042e3993_2]] is for an Officer Robert Wilson III memorial initiative on Preventing Violence Against Law Enforcement and Ensuring Officer Resilience and Survivability (VALOR).
relevance_facts.reason: The Byrne JAG program funds local law enforcement and violence prevention; the VALOR initiative directly supports officer safety and violence prevention.

source_numbers.label: Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant program

relevance_facts.fact: For the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant program, $6,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_986f1b11_1c38_4952_8425_6334042e3993_3]] is for a grant program for State and local law enforcement to provide officer training on responding to individuals with mental illness or disabilities, including for purposes described in the Law Enforcement De-Escalation Training Act of 2022.

relevance_facts.reason: This is a set-aside within a law enforcement funding stream but does not directly fund local law enforcement, violence prevention, or police hiring.

question: What FY2026 funding is available for brownfields cleanup, Superfund cleanup, or environmental remediation?
expected_divisions: DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, ENVIRONMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES
actual_divisions: DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, ENVIRONMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES

division_answers.division: DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, ENVIRONMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES
division_answers.answer:
### [INT] DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, ENVIRONMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES

Bottom line: EPA has several FY2026 brownfields, Superfund, and remediation-related funding lines, but no clean division total is available because the figures mix account totals, cleanup subamounts, grants, and fee authority.

Key buckets:
- Hazardous Substance Superfund: $282,749,000 [[num:src_int_d632d786_92bc_4a55_9797_b34bbf18c00e_1]] for necessary expenses to carry out CERCLA, including cleanup activities; also $77,100,000 [[num:src_int_8aeb2531_7161_4e19_84b4_ceb442f34014_1]] is provided under CERCLA section 311(a) and section 126(g).
- Brownfields/CERCLA grants: $98,000,000 [[num:src_int_68c231bc_233c_49a7_9433_ff67261f494c_1]] for CERCLA section 104(k) grants, plus $25,500,000 [[num:src_int_41d86abe_56ca_4f54_9ca5_8cf86e0ec3c9_1]] for CERCLA section 104(b)(8) grants; Environmental Programs and Management receives $3,114,671,000 [[num:src_int_50ecf038_8cf4_4344_8029_44323ef53133_1]], including administrative costs of the brownfields program.
- Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund Program: $88,903,000 [[num:src_int_676ecc67_2618_41b8_9ebb_1b1dcf5cd4b1_1]] for cleanup activities, including $64,583,000 [[num:src_int_676ecc67_2618_41b8_9ebb_1b1dcf5cd4b1_2]] for section 9003(h) cleanup.
- Other remediation lines: $46,250,000 [[num:src_int_5cbf3c87_b52e_4290_b96e_19388ea094b7_1]] for CERCLA section 128; $20,364,000 [[num:src_int_c33296d3_2921_4184_b50f_5116bccc7ca8_1]] for State and Tribal Assistance Grants allocated to remediation projects; $20,000,000 [[num:src_int_d0525cce_f9d7_46d6_a96c_151d49cd886d_1]] for Alaska Native contamination grants; and $2,000,000 [[num:src_int_43a8dd3d_d24d_47a3_afa5_b1919462588e_1]] for remediation of above ground leaking fuel tanks.
- EPA is also authorized to collect and obligate fees under Solid Waste Disposal Act section 3024 for FY2026.

Local caveat: Do not add the Superfund, brownfields, LUST, and other remediation lines together as one clean total; they are separate accounts/programs and include different financial types.

question: How is Department of Homeland Security funding handled in FY2026, and is there a full-year DHS amount in these laws?
expected_divisions: CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
actual_divisions: CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
answer_mode_reason: User asks about handling and existence of a full-year amount, focusing on mechanism rather than specific dollar amounts.

division_answers.division: CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
division_answers.answer:
### [CRX] CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
DHS is funded through continuing appropriations in FY2026 at the FY2025 rate for operations under the same authority and conditions for continuing projects and activities, rather than through a full-year DHS appropriation; the continuing funding was extended through January 30, 2026, and then further extended to February 13, 2026. 
- The continuing resolution covers amounts “as may be necessary” at the FY2025 rate for operations for covered DHS activities conducted in FY2025 and funded in the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (P.L. 119-4), with exceptions.
- For FEMA’s Disaster Relief Fund, amounts made available under section 101 may be apportioned up to the rate for operations necessary for Stafford Act response and recovery activities.
- A full-year DHS dollar amount was not found in the extracted facts; the laws identified here use continuing appropriations/rate-for-operations language instead.

final_answer:

- The continuing resolution covers amounts “as may be necessary” at the FY2025 rate for operations for covered DHS activities conducted in FY2025 and funded in the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (P.L. 119-4), with exceptions.
- For FEMA’s Disaster Relief Fund, amounts made available under section 101 may be apportioned up to the rate for operations necessary for Stafford Act response and recovery activities.
- A full-year DHS dollar amount was not found in the extracted facts; the laws identified here use continuing appropriations/rate-for-operations language instead.

division_answers.answer:
### [CRX] CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
The Further Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026 extends and continues federal funding on a continuing-appropriations basis, rather than providing a full-year appropriation, and carries prior-law funding forward through the specified end date.

- It amends the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026 by extending the date in section 106(3), and it covers the lapse period beginning on or about January 31, 2026.
- Its mechanism is continuing appropriations at a rate for operations set by the applicable fiscal year 2025 appropriations Acts, with the authority and conditions from those Acts carried forward.
- The Act also allows certain personnel pay and benefits amounts to be available for payments under 31 U.S.C. § 1341(c), permits limited apportionment flexibility, and ratifies obligations incurred to maintain essential activities and orderly termination of government functions.

### [CRX] CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS

question: What happens to agencies or accounts funded under the continuing resolution if no full-year appropriation is provided?
expected_divisions: CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
actual_divisions: CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
answer_mode_reason: Question asks about the effect of a continuing resolution when no full-year appropriation is provided, focusing on funding mechanism not amounts.

division_answers.division: CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
division_answers.answer:
### [CRX] CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
Bottom line: if no full-year appropriation is enacted, the continuing resolution keeps agencies/accounts operating at the applicable FY2025 rate-for-operations and under the FY2025 Act’s authority and conditions, for continuing FY2025 projects and activities, until the earliest of enactment of a project/activity appropriation, enactment of the applicable FY2026 appropriations Act without that item, or January 30, 2026.

- The Act directs only the most limited funding action permitted to continue projects and activities, and for certain programs it bars high initial rates of operation or full early distribution of grants.
- Civilian personnel pay and benefits may be apportioned up to the rate needed to avoid furloughs, and mandatory/entitlement payments continue at rates needed to maintain program levels under current law.
- Obligations for maintaining essential activities to protect life and property, and for orderly termination of government functions, are ratified; during a lapse, personnel-pay payments and certain reimbursements/compensation protections also apply.

final_answer:
### [CRX] CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
Bottom line: if no full-year appropriation is enacted, the continuing resolution keeps agencies/accounts operating at the applicable FY2025 rate-for-operations and under the FY2025 Act’s authority and conditions, for continuing FY2025 projects and activities, until the earliest of enactment of a project/activity appropriation, enactment of the applicable FY2026 appropriations Act without that item, or January 30, 2026.

- The Act directs only the most limited funding action permitted to continue projects and activities, and for certain programs it bars high initial rates of operation or full early distribution of grants.
- Civilian personnel pay and benefits may be apportioned up to the rate needed to avoid furloughs, and mandatory/entitlement payments continue at rates needed to maintain program levels under current law.
- Obligations for maintaining essential activities to protect life and property, and for orderly termination of government functions, are ratified; during a lapse, personnel-pay payments and certain reimbursements/compensation protections also apply.

## Included

- Human Foods Program and related field activities: $1,171,319,000 [[num:src_ag_b9334bc1_3b42_4f87_9b47_7824d5cc66d0_1]]

- Validation check: the listed center/activity and rent lines reconcile to the account total: $6,957,972,000 [[num:drv_recon_1]]

### Financing-source breakdown
- Prescription drug user fees: $1,556,039,000 [[num:src_ag_cee4dfd9_de7e_40f0_b82e_f896328a8490_2]]
- Medical device user fees: $478,166,000 [[num:src_ag_cee4dfd9_de7e_40f0_b82e_f896328a8490_3]]
- Human generic drug user fees: $670,900,000 [[num:src_ag_cee4dfd9_de7e_40f0_b82e_f896328a8490_4]]
- Biosimilar biological product user fees: $55,841,000 [[num:src_ag_cee4dfd9_de7e_40f0_b82e_f896328a8490_5]]
- Animal drug user fees: $36,152,000 [[num:src_ag_cee4dfd9_de7e_40f0_b82e_f896328a8490_6]]
- Generic new animal drug user fees: $26,724,000 [[num:src_ag_78bb81a7_2736_4db7_96b1_5a0e24971044_4]]
- Tobacco product user fees: $712,000,000 [[num:src_ag_78bb81a7_2736_4db7_96b1_5a0e24971044_5]]

## Not Added Separately
### Suballocations within included amounts
- $15,000,000 [[num:src_ag_b9334bc1_3b42_4f87_9b47_7824d5cc66d0_2]]: a foreign-seafood inspection set-aside within the Human Foods Program total, so it is already included in the $1,171,319,000 [[num:src_ag_b9334bc1_3b42_4f87_9b47_7824d5cc66d0_1]] line.
- $10,000,000 [[num:src_ag_b9334bc1_3b42_4f87_9b47_7824d5cc66d0_4]]: a foreign-inspection pilot set-aside within CDER, so it is already included in the $2,496,766,000 [[num:src_ag_b9334bc1_3b42_4f87_9b47_7824d5cc66d0_3]] line.
- $44,400,000 [[num:src_ag_c5f1a478_c79a_41c8_b555_a51f9d9639c7_4]]: White Oak Consolidation is a suballocation within Rent and Related activities, so it is already included in the $205,180,000 [[num:src_ag_c5f1a478_c79a_41c8_b555_a51f9d9639c7_3]] line.

### Transfers, caps, and limitations
- $25,000 [[num:src_ag_c5f1a478_c79a_41c8_b555_a51f9d9639c7_7]]: a not-to-exceed cap for official reception and representation expenses within Other activities, not a separate appropriation line.
- $2,000,000 [[num:src_ag_c5f1a478_c79a_41c8_b555_a51f9d9639c7_8]]: a transfer limit from Other activities, not new budget authority.
- $1,500,000 [[num:src_ag_c5f1a478_c79a_41c8_b555_a51f9d9639c7_9]]: a transfer out of the non-user-fee portion of Other activities to HHS OIG, not an amount to add to the account total.

### Financing-source treatment
- $200,000,000 [[num:src_ag_19c8bdaf_e285_4e2c_a7ef_1487cfebfd32_1]]: an ENDS enforcement set-aside from tobacco product user fees, already inside the $712,000,000 [[num:src_ag_78bb81a7_2736_4db7_96b1_5a0e24971044_5]] tobacco source amount.
- $2,000,000 [[num:src_ag_19c8bdaf_e285_4e2c_a7ef_1487cfebfd32_2]]: a suballocation within the $200,000,000 [[num:src_ag_19c8bdaf_e285_4e2c_a7ef_1487cfebfd32_1]] ENDS enforcement set-aside.

## Caveats
- The available text also credits several fee categories to the account without dollar amounts in this set of figures, so they are noted but not numerically broken out here.

division_answers.answer:
### [CJS] COMMERCE, JUSTICE, SCIENCE, AND RELATED AGENCIES
### [NASA] NASA

Bottom line: The available FY2026 text lists the NASA major accounts below, but it also contains suballocations, transfer limits, and one unresolved account-label inconsistency, so those items are separated out rather than summed into a single clean total.

## Included
### Programmatic breakdown
- Science: $7,250,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_eb913c86_3ab8_478b_b5b6_749cc2964621_1]]
- Aeronautics: $935,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_eb913c86_3ab8_478b_b5b6_749cc2964621_2]]
- Space Technology: $920,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_9200ba38_f0bf_4ac2_831d_340bd9add96f_2]]
- Exploration: $7,783,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_9200ba38_f0bf_4ac2_831d_340bd9add96f_3]]
- Space Operations: $4,175,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_fec2ca27_0b4c_4515_ad6f_5003a2a8257a_1]]
- Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics Engagement: $143,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_fec2ca27_0b4c_4515_ad6f_5003a2a8257a_2]]
- Safety, Security and Mission Services: $3,000,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_26c8910a_7464_4f53_94c6_6154b8528f91_1]]
- Construction and Environmental Compliance and Restoration: $185,336,000 [[num:src_cjs_49c4f821_48fe_4a63_8f9c_43fa6c39e13c_1]]
- Office of Inspector General: $46,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_49c4f821_48fe_4a63_8f9c_43fa6c39e13c_3]]

### Financing-source breakdown
- Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics Engagement joint funding: up to $5,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_716b885f_6f84_4787_bb58_1ae4601d03f9_1]] from STEM Engagement, plus up to $1,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_716b885f_6f84_4787_bb58_1ae4601d03f9_2]] each from Science, Aeronautics, Space Technology, Exploration, and Space Operations, for one joint purpose; these are cross-account contributions, not amounts to add on top of the parent accounts.
- Safety, Security and Mission Services transfer to the Working Capital Fund: up to $38,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_716b885f_6f84_4787_bb58_1ae4601d03f9_3]]; this is a transfer limit, not new budget authority.
- Construction and Environmental Compliance and Restoration lease proceeds: not to exceed $33,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_49c4f821_48fe_4a63_8f9c_43fa6c39e13c_2]]; this is a financing-source limitation inside CECR, not a separate appropriation.

## Not Added Separately
### Suballocations within included amounts
- $58,417,135 [[num:src_cjs_26c8910a_7464_4f53_94c6_6154b8528f91_2]]: SSMS community project funding / congressionally directed spending within the $3,000,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_26c8910a_7464_4f53_94c6_6154b8528f91_1]] account total, so it is already included in SSMS.
- $2,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_49c4f821_48fe_4a63_8f9c_43fa6c39e13c_4]]: the Office of Inspector General multi-year availability clause within the $46,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_49c4f821_48fe_4a63_8f9c_43fa6c39e13c_3]] account total; it does not add a separate appropriation.
- STEM Engagement table-based purpose allocations: the text says the specified purpose amounts in the explanatory statement table are minimums within the $143,000,000 account, so those purpose lines are internal allocations, not add-ons.
- CECR prior-year project use limit: the text limits the share of current-year CECR funds that may be applied to prior-year CECR projects; this is a use cap, not extra funding.

### Transfers, caps, and limitations
- NASA transfer authority: the text allows transfers between current-year NASA appropriations subject to stated percentage caps; this is an adjustment rule, not additional funding.
- CECR construction transfer cap: funds transferred into CECR for construction activities may not increase that account beyond the stated cap; this is a limit on use, not a new account amount.

### Financing-source treatment
- $5,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_716b885f_6f84_4787_bb58_1ae4601d03f9_1]] plus up to $1,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_716b885f_6f84_4787_bb58_1ae4601d03f9_2]] each from five other NASA accounts: joint STEM funding structure, not a separate pool to add again.
- $33,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_49c4f821_48fe_4a63_8f9c_43fa6c39e13c_2]]: lease proceeds used within CECR, not an extra appropriation.
- $38,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_716b885f_6f84_4787_bb58_1ae4601d03f9_3]]: transfer-out authority from SSMS, not a separate funding line.

## Caveats
- The available text also shows a separate Science figure of $7,783,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_9200ba38_f0bf_4ac2_831d_340bd9add96f_1]], with that same figure also attached to Exploration [[num:src_cjs_9200ba38_f0bf_4ac2_831d_340bd9add96f_3]] and $935,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_9200ba38_f0bf_4ac2_831d_340bd9add96f_4]] attached to Space Operations in another line; those labels are not reconciled in the provided provisions, so I am not combining them into a single NASA subtotal.
- Because of the mixed account labels and transfer/limitation language, the figures above should be read as line-item amounts and use rules, not as a fully additive budget pool.

- Aeronautics: $935,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_eb913c86_3ab8_478b_b5b6_749cc2964621_2]]
- Space Technology: $920,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_9200ba38_f0bf_4ac2_831d_340bd9add96f_2]]
- Exploration: $7,783,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_9200ba38_f0bf_4ac2_831d_340bd9add96f_3]]
- Space Operations: $4,175,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_fec2ca27_0b4c_4515_ad6f_5003a2a8257a_1]]
- Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics Engagement: $143,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_fec2ca27_0b4c_4515_ad6f_5003a2a8257a_2]]
- Safety, Security and Mission Services: $3,000,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_26c8910a_7464_4f53_94c6_6154b8528f91_1]]
- Construction and Environmental Compliance and Restoration: $185,336,000 [[num:src_cjs_49c4f821_48fe_4a63_8f9c_43fa6c39e13c_1]]
- Office of Inspector General: $46,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_49c4f821_48fe_4a63_8f9c_43fa6c39e13c_3]]

### Financing-source breakdown
- Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics Engagement joint funding: up to $5,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_716b885f_6f84_4787_bb58_1ae4601d03f9_1]] from STEM Engagement, plus up to $1,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_716b885f_6f84_4787_bb58_1ae4601d03f9_2]] each from Science, Aeronautics, Space Technology, Exploration, and Space Operations, for one joint purpose; these are cross-account contributions, not amounts to add on top of the parent accounts.
- Safety, Security and Mission Services transfer to the Working Capital Fund: up to $38,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_716b885f_6f84_4787_bb58_1ae4601d03f9_3]]; this is a transfer limit, not new budget authority.
- Construction and Environmental Compliance and Restoration lease proceeds: not to exceed $33,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_49c4f821_48fe_4a63_8f9c_43fa6c39e13c_2]]; this is a financing-source limitation inside CECR, not a separate appropriation.

## Not Added Separately
### Suballocations within included amounts
- $58,417,135 [[num:src_cjs_26c8910a_7464_4f53_94c6_6154b8528f91_2]]: SSMS community project funding / congressionally directed spending within the $3,000,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_26c8910a_7464_4f53_94c6_6154b8528f91_1]] account total, so it is already included in SSMS.
- $2,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_49c4f821_48fe_4a63_8f9c_43fa6c39e13c_4]]: the Office of Inspector General multi-year availability clause within the $46,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_49c4f821_48fe_4a63_8f9c_43fa6c39e13c_3]] account total; it does not add a separate appropriation.
- STEM Engagement table-based purpose allocations: the text says the specified purpose amounts in the explanatory statement table are minimums within the $143,000,000 account, so those purpose lines are internal allocations, not add-ons.
- CECR prior-year project use limit: the text limits the share of current-year CECR funds that may be applied to prior-year CECR projects; this is a use cap, not extra funding.

### Transfers, caps, and limitations
- NASA transfer authority: the text allows transfers between current-year NASA appropriations subject to stated percentage caps; this is an adjustment rule, not additional funding.
- CECR construction transfer cap: funds transferred into CECR for construction activities may not increase that account beyond the stated cap; this is a limit on use, not a new account amount.

### Financing-source treatment
- $5,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_716b885f_6f84_4787_bb58_1ae4601d03f9_1]] plus up to $1,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_716b885f_6f84_4787_bb58_1ae4601d03f9_2]] each from five other NASA accounts: joint STEM funding structure, not a separate pool to add again.
- $33,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_49c4f821_48fe_4a63_8f9c_43fa6c39e13c_2]]: lease proceeds used within CECR, not an extra appropriation.
- $38,500,000 [[num:src_cjs_716b885f_6f84_4787_bb58_1ae4601d03f9_3]]: transfer-out authority from SSMS, not a separate funding line.

## Caveats
- The available text also shows a separate Science figure of $7,783,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_9200ba38_f0bf_4ac2_831d_340bd9add96f_1]], with that same figure also attached to Exploration [[num:src_cjs_9200ba38_f0bf_4ac2_831d_340bd9add96f_3]] and $935,000,000 [[num:src_cjs_9200ba38_f0bf_4ac2_831d_340bd9add96f_4]] attached to Space Operations in another line; those labels are not reconciled in the provided provisions, so I am not combining them into a single NASA subtotal.
- Because of the mixed account labels and transfer/limitation language, the figures above should be read as line-item amounts and use rules, not as a fully additive budget pool.

### [AG] Rural Utilities Service — Rural Water and Waste Disposal Program Account

Bottom line: The identified provisions provide $1,015,000,000 [[num:src_ag_160a4a3e_e145_4648_b90b_06162c1802d7_1]] in direct-loan principal authority and $50,000,000 [[num:src_ag_160a4a3e_e145_4648_b90b_06162c1802d7_2]] in guaranteed-loan principal authority, which together reconcile to $1,065,000,000 [[num:drv_recon_1]] in loan authority. They also provide $445,864,564 [[num:src_ag_160a4a3e_e145_4648_b90b_06162c1802d7_3]] for the cost of direct loans, loan guarantees and grants, plus $58,900,000 [[num:drv_recon_2]] in the two technical-assistance lines. Do not add loan authority to subsidy/grant funding, and do not add nested set-asides on top of their parent amounts.

## Included
### Programmatic breakdown
- direct-loan principal authority: $1,015,000,000 [[num:src_ag_160a4a3e_e145_4648_b90b_06162c1802d7_1]]
- guaranteed-loan principal authority: $50,000,000 [[num:src_ag_160a4a3e_e145_4648_b90b_06162c1802d7_2]]

## Not Added Separately
### Suballocations within included amounts
- $3,876,000 [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_3]]: a minimum set-aside within the $51,476,000 direct-loan availability, so it is not added on top of the parent direct-loan amount
- $1,000,000 [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_4]]: also appears as the subgrant amount within the $5,000,000 section 306E allocation, so it is not counted twice
- $10,000,000 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_2]]: a suballocation within the $35,000,000 technical-assistance grants line, so it is not added separately

- $250,000 [[num:src_ag_fb4d9f83_764c_44c4_9c09_4627847af3a5_5]]: a technical-assistance set-aside within the $4,000,000 tribal business grants line, so it is not added separately
- $110,488,564 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_7]]: a suballocation within the $250,488,564 section 306(a)(2)(a) grants line, so it is not added separately

### [INT] DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, ENVIRONMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES

### [EPA] State and Tribal Assistance Grants

Bottom line: State and Tribal Assistance Grants total $4,409,609,000 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_1]]. The Clean Water and Drinking Water SRF capitalization grants total $2,764,962,000 [[num:drv_recon_1]], and the project-specific amounts below are suballocations that should not be added again.

## Included
### Programmatic breakdown
- State and Tribal Assistance Grants total: $4,409,609,000 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_1]]
- Grants under section 1459A(a) through (j) of the Safe Drinking Water Act: $28,500,000 [[num:src_int_41d86abe_56ca_4f54_9ca5_8cf86e0ec3c9_3]]
- Grants under section 1459F of the Safe Drinking Water Act: $2,250,000 [[num:src_int_43a8dd3d_d24d_47a3_afa5_b1919462588e_1]]

- Grants under section 220 of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act: $2,000,000 [[num:src_int_43a8dd3d_d24d_47a3_afa5_b1919462588e_3]]
- Grants under section 1464(d) of the Safe Drinking Water Act: $28,000,000 [[num:src_int_c33296d3_2921_4184_b50f_5116bccc7ca8_1]]
- Grants under section 1459B of the Safe Drinking Water Act: $22,000,000 [[num:src_int_c33296d3_2921_4184_b50f_5116bccc7ca8_2]]

- Grants under section 104(b)(8) of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act: $25,500,000 [[num:src_int_c33296d3_2921_4184_b50f_5116bccc7ca8_4]]
- Grants under section 221 of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act: $41,000,000 [[num:src_int_c33296d3_2921_4184_b50f_5116bccc7ca8_5]]
- Grants under section 4304(b) of the America’s Water Infrastructure Act of 2018: $5,400,000 [[num:src_int_c33296d3_2921_4184_b50f_5116bccc7ca8_6]]
- Grants under section 302(a) of the Save Our Seas 2.0 Act: $3,500,000 [[num:src_int_c33296d3_2921_4184_b50f_5116bccc7ca8_7]]
- State and Tribal Assistance Grants for congressionally directed items: $20,364,000 [[num:src_int_c33296d3_2921_4184_b50f_5116bccc7ca8_8]]
- Alaska rural water infrastructure grants: $39,000,000 [[num:src_int_68c231bc_233c_49a7_9433_ff67261f494c_1]]
- High priority water and wastewater facilities on the U.S.-Mexico Border: $35,000,000 [[num:src_int_d34f361a_4aeb_40bb_8589_d2bba8dbf995_2]]

### Financing-source breakdown
- Clean Water State Revolving Fund capitalization grants: $1,638,861,000 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_2]]
- Drinking Water State Revolving Fund capitalization grants: $1,126,101,000 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_3]]

## Not Added Separately
### Suballocations within included amounts
- $892,762,272 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_4]]: project-specific construction and water-quality protection work within the Clean Water SRF capitalization grants; already inside the parent SRF amount.
- $715,364,627 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_5]]: project-specific construction and water-quality protection work within the Drinking Water SRF capitalization grants; already inside the parent SRF amount.
- $13,300,000 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_6]] / [[num:src_int_42d8d9d1_e750_43a1_8e67_6056461cc141_1]]: administrative set-aside from the SRF capitalization-grants pool; not additional infrastructure funding.
- $1,500,000 [[num:src_int_42d8d9d1_e750_43a1_8e67_6056461cc141_2]]: Clean Watersheds Needs Survey from Clean Water SRF funds; not added on top of the SRF total.
- $30,000,000 [[num:src_int_39f46ac8_d2d9_481c_bc82_29db77a2f240_1]]: reservation for section 518(c) grants from State Revolving Funds under the Federal Water Pollution Control Act; a reservation within the CWSRF pool, not separate new funding.
- $20,000,000 [[num:src_int_39f46ac8_d2d9_481c_bc82_29db77a2f240_2]]: reservation for section 1452(i) grants from State Revolving Funds under the Safe Drinking Water Act; a reservation within the DWSRF pool, not separate new funding.
- $12,000,000 [[num:src_int_d34f361a_4aeb_40bb_8589_d2bba8dbf995_1]]: monitoring-cost reservation from Drinking Water SRF capitalization grants; not separate new funding.
- $2,000,000 [[num:src_int_fa7c2eed_58c7_4125_90f4_17f75709576e_1]]: specified uses of section 518(c) reserved funds; a use of reserved funds, not an extra appropriation.

### Financing-source treatment
- 10 percent CWSRF additional-subsidy requirement: a use restriction on the capitalization grants, not a separate dollar addition.
- 14 percent DWSRF additional-subsidy requirement: a use restriction on the capitalization grants, not a separate dollar addition.
- The DWSRF additional-subsidy share may exceed 14 percent in a lead-emergency State: this changes how the funds may be used, not the total amount appropriated.

## Caveats
- The heading contains other non-water STAG lines, but they are not counted here as part of the water-infrastructure breakdown.

question: In plain English, what does the FY2026 Agriculture division do for the FDA?
expected_divisions: AGRICULTURE, RURAL DEVELOPMENT, FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION, AND RELATED AGENCIES
actual_divisions: AGRICULTURE, RURAL DEVELOPMENT, FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION, AND RELATED AGENCIES
answer_mode_reason: User asks for plain English explanation of division's purpose for FDA.

division_answers.division: AGRICULTURE, RURAL DEVELOPMENT, FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION, AND RELATED AGENCIES
division_answers.answer:
### [AG] AGRICULTURE, RURAL DEVELOPMENT, FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION, AND RELATED AGENCIES
In plain English, the division funds FDA’s day-to-day operations through the Salaries and Expenses account, using a mix of appropriations and user fees. It covers major FDA centers and activities such as food, drugs, biologics, devices, tobacco, veterinary medicine, toxicology, rent, and other operating costs, and includes a $1,171,319,000 [[num:src_ag_78bb81a7_2736_4db7_96b1_5a0e24971044_1]] set-aside for the Human Foods Program and related field activities.

It also provides money for FDA facilities, requires regular reporting on spending and staffing, and imposes policy limits and directives such as restricting work on long-term sodium-reduction guidelines until an impact assessment is completed, while directing FDA to strengthen certain enforcement and retailer-education efforts.

final_answer:
### [AG] AGRICULTURE, RURAL DEVELOPMENT, FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION, AND RELATED AGENCIES
In plain English, the division funds FDA’s day-to-day operations through the Salaries and Expenses account, using a mix of appropriations and user fees. It covers major FDA centers and activities such as food, drugs, biologics, devices, tobacco, veterinary medicine, toxicology, rent, and other operating costs, and includes a $1,171,319,000 [[num:src_ag_78bb81a7_2736_4db7_96b1_5a0e24971044_1]] set-aside for the Human Foods Program and related field activities.

It also provides money for FDA facilities, requires regular reporting on spending and staffing, and imposes policy limits and directives such as restricting work on long-term sodium-reduction guidelines until an impact assessment is completed, while directing FDA to strengthen certain enforcement and retailer-education efforts.

question: What kinds of projects or activities does the Energy and Water Development division generally support?
expected_divisions: ENERGY AND WATER DEVELOPMENT AND RELATED AGENCIES
actual_divisions: ENERGY AND WATER DEVELOPMENT AND RELATED AGENCIES
answer_mode_reason: User asks for general description of supported projects/activities, not a dollar amount or breakdown.

division_answers.division: ENERGY AND WATER DEVELOPMENT AND RELATED AGENCIES
division_answers.answer:
### [EWD] ENERGY AND WATER DEVELOPMENT AND RELATED AGENCIES
The division generally supports water resources and civil works work such as river and harbor improvements, flood and storm damage reduction, shore protection, aquatic ecosystem restoration, navigation/channel work, flood control and coastal emergencies, and Corps of Engineers administration and emergency operations. It also supports water storage, water treatment and groundwater projects, habitat restoration, and cleanup or remedial programs for navigable waters, wetlands, and formerly utilized atomic-energy sites.

It also funds a broad set of energy and nuclear activities, including energy efficiency and renewable energy, electricity and grid deployment, nuclear energy, loan guarantees for innovative or advanced nuclear technologies, tribal and Indian energy programs, ARPA-E, cybersecurity and emergency response, nuclear waste disposal, environmental cleanup, and related defense nuclear activities. Related functions include FERC, the Energy Information Administration, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board.

final_answer:

Related functions include FERC, the Energy Information Administration, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board.

division_answers.answer:
### [INT] DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, ENVIRONMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES
The retrieved FY2026 facts show EPA treating water infrastructure as a mix of core financing and targeted grant programs: State Revolving Funds, drinking-water and clean-water set-asides, Alaska and U.S.-Mexico border water/wastewater grants, Great Lakes and watershed restoration, and WIFIA loan support. EPA also includes policy conditions that steer SRF money toward green infrastructure, water/energy efficiency, innovative projects, additional subsidy, and certain tribal, territorial, and emergency-related uses.

I do not have retrieved USDA or Energy-Water water infrastructure provisions in this fact set, so I can only summarize the EPA treatment here.

division_answers.answer:
### [EWD] ENERGY AND WATER DEVELOPMENT AND RELATED AGENCIES
FY2026 Energy-Water appropriations support water infrastructure mainly through Corps of Engineers civil works and Reclamation financing tools. The bill funds Corps activities for navigation, flood and storm damage reduction, shore protection, and aquatic ecosystem restoration, and it also provides Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Program support for direct loans and loan guarantees for water projects, including dam and levee safety projects.[[num:src_ewd_3b1cadaf_7d55_41a5_aa33_d47df2fc555e_1]]

The bill also places limits on how these water-related funds can be moved or repurposed, requiring prior Appropriations Committee approval for certain reprogramming actions and larger transfers.[[num:src_ewd_d21cf343_9f1f_427b_a9cd_e141c4814ca5_3]] The extracted facts provided here do not include direct FY2026 USDA or EPA water-infrastructure appropriations, so I can’t summarize those agencies from this record.

final_answer:
## Answer
FY2026 appropriations treat water infrastructure differently across the three bills, but with a common theme of pairing core financing with targeted support.

- **USDA** emphasizes **rural water and wastewater systems**, centered on the Rural Water and Waste Disposal Program Account at $445,864,564 [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_1]]. The agriculture bill also supports **technical assistance and system support**, including technical assistance grants at $35,000,000 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_1]], circuit riders at $23,900,000 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_4]], and grassroots source water protection at $7,500,000 [[num:src_ag_dd412d45_228f_441b_a6ec_7436bc3c39cc_1]].
- **EPA** treats water infrastructure as a mix of **large-scale state revolving fund capitalization, specialized water grants, and policy set-asides/conditions**. The division-level answer highlights State Revolving Funds, drinking-water and clean-water set-asides, Alaska and U.S.-Mexico border water and wastewater grants, Great Lakes and watershed restoration, and WIFIA loan support, while also steering some funding toward **green infrastructure, water and energy efficiency, innovative projects, and certain tribal, territorial, and emergency-related uses**.
- **Energy-Water** supports water infrastructure mainly through **Corps of Engineers civil works and Reclamation-related financing tools**, with a focus on **navigation, flood and storm damage reduction, shore protection, and aquatic ecosystem restoration**. It also includes Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Program support at $2,200,000 [[num:src_ewd_3b1cadaf_7d55_41a5_aa33_d47df2fc555e_1]] and places tighter controls on moving funds, including committee approval requirements for certain reprogrammings and transfers above $500,000 [[num:src_ewd_d21cf343_9f1f_427b_a9cd_e141c4814ca5_3]].

In plain English: **USDA is focused on rural utility systems and hands-on assistance, EPA is the main hub for broad national water-infrastructure financing and targeted water grants, and Energy-Water focuses on major federal water works and related financing authorities.**

question: What is the difference between regular appropriations and continuing appropriations in the FY2026 laws?
expected_divisions: CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
actual_divisions: CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
answer_mode_reason: User asks about the difference between types of appropriations, not about specific amounts.

division_answers.division: CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
division_answers.answer:
### [CRX] CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
Bottom line: in the FY2026 laws, **regular appropriations** are the normal full-year appropriations for the fiscal year, while **continuing appropriations** are temporary stopgap funding that keeps projects and activities running at a prior-year rate until a later appropriation is enacted or the stopgap expires. [Direct facts]

- Continuing appropriations provide “such amounts as may be necessary, at a rate for operations” under the applicable FY2025 appropriations Acts and conditions, for FY2025 activities not otherwise specifically provided for in the FY2026 act. [Section 101]
- They can cover personnel pay, allowances, and benefits; mandatory payments; essential activities; and orderly termination of government functions during a lapse, and they may be charged to later-enacted applicable appropriations when that bill becomes law. [Sections 103, 104, 107, 108, 111, 112]
- Regular appropriations are described here as full fiscal-year appropriations, in contrast to the pro rata, time-limited continuing appropriations tied to prior-year rates and extension dates. [Direct facts]

final_answer:
### [CRX] CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
Bottom line: in the FY2026 laws, **regular appropriations** are the normal full-year appropriations for the fiscal year, while **continuing appropriations** are temporary stopgap funding that keeps projects and activities running at a prior-year rate until a later appropriation is enacted or the stopgap expires. [Direct facts]

- Continuing appropriations provide “such amounts as may be necessary, at a rate for operations” under the applicable FY2025 appropriations Acts and conditions, for FY2025 activities not otherwise specifically provided for in the FY2026 act. [Section 101]
- They can cover personnel pay, allowances, and benefits; mandatory payments; essential activities; and orderly termination of government functions during a lapse, and they may be charged to later-enacted applicable appropriations when that bill becomes law. [Sections 103, 104, 107, 108, 111, 112]
- Regular appropriations are described here as full fiscal-year appropriations, in contrast to the pro rata, time-limited continuing appropriations tied to prior-year rates and extension dates. [Direct facts]

division_answers.answer:
### [THUD] TRANSPORTATION, HOUSING AND URBAN DEVELOPMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES
The FY2026 Transportation-HUD division covers major local-government and public-agency housing programs, including the Public Housing Fund at $8,319,393,000 [[num:src_thud_9841cfd4_18e8_4504_8843_461e06569ba5_1]], the Fair Housing Initiatives Program at $56,000,000 [[num:src_thud_00d60c71_1e93_4442_82ea_090e0e38e484_1]], lead hazard reduction and healthy homes at $295,600,000 [[num:src_thud_00d60c71_1e93_4442_82ea_090e0e38e484_7]], Choice Neighborhoods at $25,000,000 [[num:src_thud_f70814d7_3213_4d74_969b_06ce52e722c1_1]], and comprehensive local planning grants of up to $10,000,000 [[num:src_thud_15a1a1b4_ea5d_418a_a73c_5f14b977350a_1]]. It also includes self-sufficiency funding of $206,400,000 [[num:src_thud_15a1a1b4_ea5d_418a_a73c_5f14b977350a_2]] and transition grants and other Homeless Assistance Grants provisions for continuum-of-care recipients.

On the transportation side, the division includes Grants-In-Aid for Airports at $577,356,000 [[num:src_thud_08e7ebfb_009f_4360_b8cf_a3a46fff4355_1]], electric vehicle charging infrastructure at $503,756,000 [[num:src_thud_7f4b5b98_bc4a_48c2_b1fc_52cf3013c4b7_1]], truck-emissions reduction at port facilities at $90,000,000 [[num:src_thud_7f4b5b98_bc4a_48c2_b1fc_52cf3013c4b7_2]], and a $100,000,000 [[num:src_thud_11dc667c_46a9_481c_862a_e74f874f7310_1]] transfer for natural gas distribution infrastructure safety grants. It also provides formula-grant adjustment authority, some flexibility for public housing agencies and Moving to Work agencies, and quarterly reporting and grant-transparency requirements for DOT and HUD.
